exclude: runtime: working copy of characters 64-127 (the background tiles), rewritten each round from $EA00, $EC00 or $EE00 by $F552 and $9C59
extra: an unused variant of characters 128-255, outside the character window; no instruction reads it

comments.text: Save the current player's wall from the screen into that player's 160-byte wall buffer (pointer from wall_buffer_lo/hi indexed by current_player), so it can be rebuilt when that player's turn comes back. Called from $9B67 when a life is lost. For each of the 16 brick rows (row_counter 1..16, screen row address from the table at $F78B, colour RAM at the same offset in $D800): bytes 0-1 of the row record get one bit per brick (13 bricks, every second screen column from column 1, bit set when the character is $80 or above, i.e. a brick, shifted to bits 15..3); bytes 2-9 get one colour nibble per brick (colour RAM & 7, or for colour 9 cells 1 / 9 / $0A by character: below $82, $82-$85 silver, $86 and above gold), built in row_nibbles ($0264). Same record layout as the round layouts at $8000 that rebuild_wall ($F371/$F3C2) reads. Uses $0D/$0E (screen), $0F/$10 (colour RAM), $11/$12 (buffer), $0211/$0212 (bit accumulator).
One brick row: clear the 16-bit presence accumulator $0211/$0212, then take the screen row's address from $F78B + 2*row_counter, plus 1 (column 1 holds the left half of brick 0).
BIT $EA18 skips the CLC: carry = 1 when the character is a brick ($80+), 0 otherwise
Colour nibbles of the row's 13 bricks into row_nibbles, then packed two to a byte into record bytes 2..9; after the row the record pointer $11/$12 moves on 10 bytes and row_counter counts to 16.
BIT $0AA9 is a skip: the bytes $A9 $0A are LDA #$0A, reached by the BCS at $068A for gold bricks (character $86 or above); $0AA9 itself is never meant to be read

Split pointer table, two entries: low bytes $59 $F9, high bytes (at $06CF) $04 $04. Entry n is player n's saved-wall buffer: player 1 at $0459, player 2 at $04F9. Read by save_wall_of_player ($0608, $060D) and the wall rebuild at $F374/$F379.
High bytes of the two saved-wall buffer pointers ($04, $04); low bytes at wall_buffer_lo.

The sprite animation played over the title picture before round 1 (called once per game from $F03F, after the menu and the story; the screen is the bank-1 bitmap, so intro_sprite_setup first points the sprite multiplexer at $63F8). It drives three of the ball slots with the ball-movement code: slot 2 an attacking craft that flies a 25-point path (intro_attacker_path), shape $B4+step; at step 12 slot 1, a shot (shape $CD), leaves it and falls on the ship at X $A0, Y $87; when the shot reaches Y $A0, intro_show_patch shows two black sprites there and slot 0, the Vaus (shapes $A2-$B3, tumbling and shrinking), flies off toward X $50, Y $60. Ends when the path is done and the Vaus has run through its frames: intro_attacker_path then pulls this routine's return address and returns to $F042. Story reading of the shapes: the shapes are the bank-1 sprites at $6880-$7540, rendered and judged by eye, not watched live.
Once a frame (wait_frame at $B472): step the attacker's path, launch or land the shot, move the three ball slots, animate the escaping Vaus. Leaves only through the PLA/PLA/RTS at $0778.

The shot. Nothing before path step 12. At step 12, if ball slot 1 is idle: put the steering target (object 0) on the ship at X $A0, Y $87, start slot 1 (speed 2, sprite pointer $CD) 6 pixels left of and 6 above the attacker ($9437 + 6, $944F - 6), aim it with $B3FA. After step 12: once the shot is at Y $A0 or below, stop it, show the patch (intro_show_patch) and launch the Vaus in slot 0 from X $A0, Y $87 toward X $50, Y $60, speed 0, first shape $A2.

Path finished: clear $0276 (slot 2's active flag), give slot 2 the empty shape $D5; return while the Vaus (slot 0) is still flying, otherwise drop the caller's return address so that the RTS leaves intro_escape_animation.

The attacker's path, one waypoint per call when reached. intro_step ($0233) 0: start ball slot 2 at X $40, Y $F0 (below the picture), shape $B4, aimed at X $A0, Y $87 (object 0, shape $D5, the steering target), and step 1. Later steps: when the attacker's X equals intro_path_x[step], move to the next step: the target becomes (intro_path_x, intro_path_y) of the new step, the attacker's speed intro_path_speed and its shape $B4 + step, and re-aim it ($B3FA). At step 25 (intro_path_done) it hides the attacker and, once the Vaus has finished, leaves intro_escape_animation.
Step 0 of the path: attacker at X $40, Y $F0; steering target at X $A0, Y $87 with the empty shape $D5; slot 0 given shape $B4 (overwritten when the Vaus launches); aim and step to 1.

Intro path, Y of each waypoint, indexed by intro_step 1-24 (29 bytes; entry 0 and entries 25-28 are not read): from $FA rising to $6F. The steering target is put here when the attacker reaches the previous waypoint.

Intro path, X of each waypoint, indexed by intro_step 0-24 (29 bytes, entries 25-28 not read): $40 $42 ... $7E, then back down to $6B. The step advances when the attacker's X equals this value exactly, so a waypoint passed without an exact hit would stall the path (the Bresenham steps move one pixel at a time on the major axis, so it is hit).

Intro path, attacker speed per waypoint (extra Bresenham steps per frame, into the ball speed $0261+2), indexed by intro_step 1-24: 0 for steps 1-12, 2 for 13-15, 1 for 16-17, 0 after (28 bytes to $0831).

Test one key of the keyboard matrix. In: A = key number, 8 x row + column (the KERNAL's numbering: row selects the $DC00 bit through key_row_select, column the $DC01 bit through key_col_mask). Out: carry set when that key is down. A column bit that also reads low with no row selected is a joystick in port 1 (or another key line held), not the key, and returns carry clear. Leaves $DC00 = $7F and $DC01 = $FF; Y preserved through key_y_save ($0213). Callers: the menu ($B5A1, keys N J K P 1 2 D), the keyboard control ($FD82 left SHIFT $0F, $FD8E right SHIFT $34).
Eight $DC00 values, one keyboard row driven low each: $FE $FD $FB $F7 $EF $DF $BF $7F, indexed by key number / 8.
Eight $DC01 bit masks, $01 to $80, indexed by key number AND 7.

Move the intro's three ball slots, 2 down to 0: each active slot ($0274,x) takes 1 + speed ($0261,x) Bresenham steps through $A2DB. Slot 0, the Vaus, moves only on frames where bit 1 of frame_counter has changed since last time (intro_slot0_tick), i.e. every second frame.

Animate the escaping Vaus: every fourth frame (bit 2 of frame_counter changed, kept in intro_frame_tick $021F) advance slot 0's sprite pointer ($F82D); after shape $B3 give it the empty shape $D5 and stop the slot.

Sprites for the intro over the title bitmap: patch the multiplexer's pointer stores ($FC17 and $F976, high bytes of STA $C3FA,Y-style operands) to $63 so that sprite pointers go to $63F8, the bank-1 screen of the title; enable sprites 2-7 in multicolour, clear the X high bits, clear X positions of objects 0-11 ($942D-$9438), sprite multicolours $D025 = 3 (cyan) and $D026 = $0A (light red), colour 1 (white) for objects 8-10 ($F821-$F823), colour 0 (black) for objects 2-3 ($F81B/$F81C).

Put objects 2 and 3 at X $A0, Y $87 and Y $9F with shapes $A0 and $A1 (black, set by intro_sprite_setup): two stacked sprites at the spot where the Vaus leaves the ship. Assumed to cover the Vaus drawn in the bitmap; not checked live.
Self-modified operand: $262B writes the tune tempo (low nibble of the tune record byte 6) here, so ADC #tempo builds the note-length table $254A-$2569 as tempo, 2*tempo, 3*tempo ...

Title picture, multicolour bitmap (video bank 1, shown with $D018 bits 4-7 = 8 and bit 3 = 0 from $B48C, $DD00 = $C2 from $B487): 8000 bytes, 8 per character cell, cells in screen order; pixel pair 00 = $D021, 01 = colour matrix high nibble ($6000), 10 = its low nibble, 11 = colour RAM (copied from $6400 by $B499). Rows 0-2: top of the ARKANOID logo, and IMAGINE / TAITO in yellow at the right. No instruction reads it; only the video chip does
Title bitmap rows 3-5 ($43C0-$477F): the middle of the ARKANOID logo, its O drawn as a gridded sphere, on the starfield
Title bitmap rows 6-8 ($4780-$4B3F): the lower edge of the ARKANOID logo and open starfield

A byte of the title bitmap (row 6, column 5, pixel line 1). It carries a name only because of the skip trick at $9F9E: BEQ $9FA6 lands inside BIT $47A9 ($2C $A9 $47) and runs LDA #$47; the other path runs LDA #$AF, then the BIT, which only sets flags. No instruction reads this byte as data
Title bitmap rows 9-11 ($4B40-$4EFF): starfield, then the top of the grey mothership rising into row 11
Title bitmap rows 12-14 ($4F00-$52BF): the mothership's grey upper hull and its central dome, on the starfield
Title bitmap rows 15-17 ($52C0-$567F): the mothership's hull and its left cannon banks; the upper tip of the Vaus (blue and purple, at the right edge) begins
Title bitmap rows 18-20 ($5680-$5A3F): the mothership's lower hull and cannons with their yellow muzzles; the body of the Vaus at the right
Title bitmap rows 21-23 ($5A40-$5DFF): the mothership's lowest cannon pair and stern; the lower end of the Vaus at the right
Title bitmap row 24, the last ($5E00-$5F3F): starfield and the artist's signature "Jones" in white at the bottom right

Start of the self-erasing protection area $5F40-$5F86, which the loop at $5F86 fills with $01 when the check passes, so after start-up every byte here reads $01. These two bytes ($44 $45, an undocumented NOP $45) never run: the routine is entered at $5F42 from $B9DE

Copy protection, called once from the start-up at $B9DE. Writes 1 to CIA 1 timer A low ($DC04), control $D9 to $DC0E, calls $A949 (decrypts $BA0A-$BA6A by XOR with $A71A-$A77A), then writes A to the serial data register $DC0C and loops: restart the timer ($DC0E = $D9), wait for the timer A bit (bit 0) in $DC0D, keep the whole interrupt register in $BA65, and start again unless the serial-port bit (bit 3) is also set. On a machine whose serial port never completes, this hangs. Then it waits three more timer underflows ($5F72), writes $DC0C again, and overwrites $5F40-$5F86 (itself, up to the STA $DC0C) with $01 (A = 1 from the AND #$01). Returns with X = $FF. Undocumented NOPs at $5F44 and $5F4E pad it to mislead a disassembler
$44 $6D: undocumented NOP $6D (zero-page read, 2 bytes), does nothing; executed (simulator) between LDA #$01 and STA $DC04

$1C $AD $08: undocumented NOP $08AD,X (absolute,X read, 3 bytes), does nothing; executed between STA $DC0E and JSR $A949. A documented-only disassembler shows the $AD as LDA $2008 and misreads the JSR
serial-port wait loop: restart timer A, poll $DC0D, store it in $BA65 (read back by $5F66 and later code)
self-erase: X = $46 down to 0 stores A ($01) at $5F40-$5F86; the loop itself ($5F88-$5F8E) survives

113 bytes equal, byte for byte, to the title colour matrix at $604F-$60BF: $5F40-$5FFF lies $C0 below $6000-$60BF and once held the same bytes; the protection routine at $5F40-$5F8E was written over the first 79. No code found that reads $5F8F-$5FFF (simulator read map, opcodes.py --refs); a leftover of how the image was built

Title picture colour matrix (the video matrix of bank 1 at $6000, $D018 = $80 from $B48C): 1000 bytes, one per cell, 40 x 25; high nibble = colour of pixel pair 01, low nibble = colour of pair 10 in the bitmap at $4000. High nibbles mostly $0 (black) and $F (light grey), low nibbles mostly $0, $6 (blue) and $F. Read only by the video chip

16 bytes after the colour matrix, before the sprite pointers: not displayed and not read by any code found. Together with $63F8-$63FA they equal $6400-$6412, the start of the colour-RAM source, as loaded

Sprite pointers of video bank 1 (matrix $6000 + $3F8), one per sprite 0-7; value v shows the 64 bytes at $4000 + 64v. Used while the title is the background of the intro animation: $08CC writes $63 into the operand high bytes $FC17 and $F976 of the multiplexer stores STA $C3FA,Y at $FC15 and $F974, which then fill $63FB-$63FF (sprites 3-7) from the table $F825 (simulator: values $A0-$D5, the frames at $6800-$757F, and $40 four times). $F07D puts $C3 back for play (pointers at $C3F8). As loaded they hold $56 $D6 $06 $A0 $A1 $D5 $D5 $D5: the file was saved with sprites 3 and 4 on frames $A0/$A1 and 5-7 on the blank frame $D5

Title colour-RAM source, 1024 bytes, copied page by page to $D800-$DBFF by $B499-$B4B4 when the title is shown; only the low nibble reaches colour RAM, the colour of pixel pair 11 in each cell. This page: cells 0-255 (rows 0 to 6, column 15): the logo's orange-red outline ($A) on blue ($6)
Title colour-RAM source, cells 256-511 (row 6 column 16 to row 12 column 31), to $D900: the logo's lower edge and the top of the mothership
Title colour-RAM source, cells 512-767 (row 12 column 32 to row 19 column 7), to $DA00: the mothership's hull ($C, $B, $F greys) and the top of the Vaus
Title colour-RAM source, cells 768-999 (row 19 column 8 to the end) to $DB00-$DBE7, then 24 bytes $67E8-$67FF that the same loop copies to the unused colour RAM $DBE8-$DBFF

Screen memory, 1000 cells ($C000-$C3E7), bank 3. Runtime state: $B6F0 fills it with $1C (and colour RAM with 3) and the menu, story and play screens are drawn over that; the loaded bytes, a copy of the menu, are overwritten before they are shown. Row 0 is the top wall: $F64F copies 28 chars from $F6DE into $C000-$C01B.
Screen row 1: $F655-$F65A OR $10 into its first 28 cells, turning the background tiles $40-$4F into their shaded twins $50-$5F under the top wall.
Screen row 4, columns 31-36: the high score's six digits, written by $FB2F-$FB4D from BCD $0941-$0943 (digit + $30).
Screen row 5, columns 11-16: the first of ten rows (5-14) that $970B saves to $02B0-$02EB, six cells each.
Screen row 6, column 9: the base address of the second of $B6F0's four 250-cell fills, which covers $C0FA-$C1F3.
Screen row 6, columns 11-16, saved by $9713 to $02B6.
Screen row 7, columns 11-16, saved by $9719 to $02BC.
Screen row 8, columns 11-16, saved by $971F to $02C2.
Screen row 9, columns 11-16, saved by $9725 to $02C8.
Screen row 9, columns 31-36: player 1's score, six digits written by $FB4F-$FB6D from BCD $0927-$0929.
Screen row 10, columns 11-16, saved by $972B to $02CE.
Screen row 10, column 13: top-left cell of the 2x2-char picture $9824 draws from the table at $987E (char n, n+1 above n+2, n+3).
Screen row 10, column 14: top-right cell of $9824's 2x2 picture; on the menu, $B631 writes the number of devices here ($0940 + $31).
Screen row 10, columns 37-38: player 1's lives, from BCD $0936 (written at $FA62 and $FA76); the tens digit and a $99 value print as blanks.
Screen row 10, column 38: player 1 lives, units digit ($FA76; blank when $0936 = $99).
Screen row 11, columns 11-16, saved by $9731 to $02D4.
Screen row 11, column 13: bottom-left cell of $9824's 2x2 picture.
Screen row 11, column 14: bottom-right cell of $9824's 2x2 picture.
Screen row 11, columns 37-38: player 1's round, $093D + 1 in decimal, written by $F39B.
Screen row 11, column 38: player 1 round, units digit ($F3A4).
Screen row 12, columns 11-16, saved by $9737 to $02DA.
Screen row 12, column 14: on the menu, the number of players ($0939 + $31), written by $B628.
Screen row 12, column 19: the base of the third of $B6F0's four 250-cell fills ($C1F4-$C2ED).
Screen row 13, columns 11-16, saved by $973D to $02E0.
Screen row 14, columns 11-16, saved by $9743 to $02E6, the last row of $970B's save.
Screen row 18, column 29: the base of the last of $B6F0's four 250-cell fills ($C2EE-$C3E7).
Screen row 18, columns 31-36: player 2's score, six digits written by $FB6F onward from BCD $092A-$092C.
Screen row 19: $9BAE prints a message from the table at $9DD6 here (the GAME OVER messages, PETSCII AND $3F, spaces as $1C), with colours at $DAD0, $DAF8 and $DB20.
Screen row 19, columns 37-38: player 2's lives, from BCD $0937 (written at $FA8D and $FAA1).
Screen row 19, column 38: player 2 lives, units digit ($FAA1; blank when $0937 = $99).
Screen row 20, columns 37-38: player 2's round, $093E + 1 in decimal, written by $F3AE-$F3BE.
Screen row 20, column 38: player 2 round, units digit ($F3B7).
Screen rows 22-24, column 27 ($C38B, $C3B3, $C3DB): the right wall's exit, given chars $E8, $E9, $EA by $F6B4-$F6BE.
Screen row 23, column 27: the exit's middle cell, char $E9 ($F6BA).
Screen row 24, column 27: the exit's bottom cell, char $EA ($F6BE).
Sprite pointers ($C3F8-$C3FF, screen + $3F8): shape = $C000 + value x 64. Sprite 0 is set to $96 here by $F25D.
Sprite 1's pointer, set to $97 by $F262.
Sprite pointers 2-7, rewritten many times a frame by the multiplexer at $F974 and $FC15 from the table at $F825 (with colours from $F819 into $D029,Y).

1 KB of character data laid out like chars 128-255 ($CC00-$CFFF) but not the same: chars 128-145 here are flat blocks where $CC00 has shaded bricks, and about a dozen others differ. Outside the character window ($D018 puts chars at $C800) and not referenced by any instruction found; only the first $29 bytes are read, by the collision code at $A28B-$A2C3 when it looks below the screen's last row (sim). Probably an earlier version left in the image; not checked further.

The play, menu and story character set, chars 0-31 ($C800-$C8FF), hi-res: $00 is the copyright sign, $01-$1A the letters A-Z, $1B a symbol, $1C the blank the game prints for a space ($B65E, $9BAC), $1D-$1F the first ARKANOID logo pieces. Bank 3 with $D018 = $02 ($B543) or $03: chars at $C800. Never written: authored data.

charset chars 32-63 ($C900-$C9FF): $20-$28 more ARKANOID logo pieces, $29-$2F other graphics (the logo at the top right of the play screen also uses $A8-$AB, $B4, $B7, $BA, $C8, $C9), $30-$39 the digits 0-9 (the score code adds $30 to a digit), $3A a quote mark, $3B-$3D panel-box edges, $3E/$3F the 1 and 2 after PLAYER.

Chars 64-95 of the live character set: the background tiles, rewritten from tiles_set_a ($EC00) or tiles_set_b ($EE00) by $F552 at each round, or from tiles_round33 ($EA00) by $9C59. Runtime state; at the hand-over it holds a copy of $EC00.
Chars 96-127 of the live character set, the second half of the background tile set, written by $F552 or $9C59 like $CA00.

Chars 128-255 of the live character set, multicolour, in place as loaded: bricks and play-screen furniture. On round 1's screen bricks are pairs such as $80/$81 and $85/$89. $9C59 reloads chars 128-255 from $1C00-$1FFF (nearly identical) for the round with index $20.
charset_upper chars 160-191 ($CD00-$CDFF): the ARKANOID logo pieces $A8-$AB, $B4, $B7, $BA; panel-box edges $B2, $B3, $B8, $B9; and the big PLAYER lettering $BD-$C6 ($BD-$BF here).

charset_upper chars 192-223 ($CE00-$CEFF): the rest of the PLAYER lettering ($C0-$C6), $C7 the menu's selection mark ($B61E), $C8/$C9 logo pieces, and $CA-$D9, four frames of a 2x2-char picture that $9824 draws at screen rows 10-11, columns 13-14 from the table at $987E.

charset_upper chars 224-255 ($CF00-$CFFF): the playfield walls. Left wall $F1-$F5, right wall $F6-$FA, top wall $FC with corners $FB and $FF, the two enemy gates in the top wall ($EB $EC $EB at columns 6-8, $FD $FE $FD at columns 19-21), and the exit cells $E8-$EA in the right wall.

Chars $E8-$EA ($CF40-$CF57): the three cells of the exit in the right wall (screen rows 22-24, column 27, placed by $F6B1). $F6C2 makes them look like wall by copying chars $F6-$F8 over them; $A428 copies the open-exit chars $ED-$EF over them and colours the cells 9; $A45A then moves the 24 bytes on by one address per call (one pixel row down the three stacked cells, the last byte wrapping to the first), the open exit's animation.
Byte 1 of char $E8: the target of $A463 (STA $CF41,Y), the one-byte rotation of the exit chars that $A45A runs.
Last byte of char $EA: $A45A saves it before the rotation and puts it back in $CF40, closing the loop.

Chars $EB-$EC ($CF58-$CF67): the left enemy gate in the top wall. $F0B4 sets them and the right gate's chars to the closed pattern from $9950-$995F; $98D8-$993D blank or restore them row by row from the middle out, the gate opening and closing.
Char $EC ($CF60-$CF67), the middle of the left gate, written with $CF58 by $98EB/$98F1 and $9931/$993D.
Chars $ED-$EF ($CF68-$CF7F): the open exit's pattern, copied over chars $E8-$EA by $A428.

Chars $F6-$F8 ($CFB0-$CFC7): right-wall chars, the source $F6C2 copies over the exit chars. It also colours the three cells $0E. Its loop runs Y from $18 down to 0, 25 bytes, so it also copies $CFC8 (row 0 of char $F9) over $CF58 (row 0 of the left gate's char $EB).
Chars $FD-$FE ($CFE8-$CFF7): the right enemy gate in the top wall, set to the closed pattern from $9950 by $F0B4 with the left gate.

Sprites $40-$41 ($D000-$D07F), multicolour: the Vaus, left half (rounded end and body) and right half (body and rounded end), drawn in rows 12-20 of each slot. $40 and $41 appear in the multiplexer's pointer table at $F825 and in sprite pointers 2-7 (sim, round 1 and attract). Bank 3: the video chip reads this RAM while the CPU sees the VIC-II and SID here, so no instruction reads it by address. The 64th byte of every slot in $D000-$E9FF is padding the video chip never shows.
Sprite $41 ($D040): the Vaus, right half; spr_vaus ($40) is the left.

Sprite $42 ($D080-$D0BF): the ball, a few pixels in the top rows of the slot. $F267 stores $42 into three multiplexer entries ($F829-$F82B), one per ball; play-ram shows $42 in three of the sprite pointers.

Sprite $94 ($E500-$E53F): the blank capsule, a rounded bar 10 rows tall. $A7E9 builds the lettered capsule (sprite $95) from it each frame, reading its middle byte column ($E501,x).
Middle byte of row 0 of spr_capsule: the base of $A7F6's read, LDA $E501,X with X = 0, 3 .. 27.

Sprite $95 ($E540-$E57F): the capsule with its letter, rebuilt by $A7E9: for ten rows, $E541,x = ($E501,x AND $A850,y) OR $A80F,y, with Y stepping through eight rows from $0238 so that the letter scrolls round. Runtime state: play-ram differs from the hand-over here. The simulator wrote $95 to sprite pointers 2-7.
Middle byte of row 0 of spr_capsule_letter: the base of $A7FF's write, STA $E541,X.

Sprites $96-$97 ($E580-$E5FF): the working copy of sprite 0 and 1's shape. $F25D sets pointers 0/1 to $96/$97 and $F24A makes both sprites black; they are hi-res ($D01C bits 0-1 clear in the play frame). Restored from spr_frame_master by $F09E, cleared to zero by $F0AA (called through $96D7), and $A4C4 ORs one-pixel masks from $FC91 ($80, $40 .. $01) into it, ten rows per call once the X position at $9446 passes $E0. Together the two halves draw a box outline on a striped base; what it depicts is not established.
Sprite $97, the right half of spr_frame_work. $A4DD-$A4E3 OR a mask from $FC91 into it, every third byte from a row given by $0247/8.
Sprite $97 row 1, byte 0. $A4D6 tests it for $FF: once it is full, $A4FB goes on to OR the mask into the left half ($E580) instead.
Sprites $98-$99 ($E600-$E67F): the master of sprites 0 and 1's shape, copied whole into spr_frame_work ($E580) by $F09E. The pointer values $98/$99 themselves were never seen in a sprite pointer.
Sprite $99 ($E640-$E67F): the right half of spr_frame_master, copied to $E5C0 by $F09E.
